newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Telecom giants flock to Brazil cellphone bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Telecom giants flock to Brazil cellphone bid.

text.p: Brazil took a big step towards privatizating its huge telecommunications industry Monday when it received bids from 15 groups interested in multi-billion-dollar opportunities in cellular services.

Executives from some of the world's leading telecom companies hauled heavy boxes stuffed with technical data to the Communications Ministry, where the lengthy procedure of checking the bidders and their proposals got underway.
"Lots of countries used to have this kind of potential," said Robert Meyer, BellSouth Corp's director of Latin American business development. "A big market with low penetration is very interesting."

Other international telecom giants bidding include AirTouch Communications Inc, SBC Communications Inc and other U.S. firms; Canada's BCE Inc ; Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa ; Italy's Stet SpA; and a host of others.

"This is a giant step towards privatization," said Antonio Carlos Rego Gil, whose Teldin telecommunications company has joined forces with France Telecom and a local bank's investment funds to bid for concessions.

Brazil expects to raise about $100 billion by privatizing its telecommuncations industry over the next few years, starting with concessions to run so-called B Band cellular services in 10 regional blocks. Private operators of B Band services will compete with existing A Band services provided by the state-level units of federally owned Telebras, which will be privatized from next year.

The B Band operators will be allowed to hold a maximum of two concessions each -- one in a developed region, the other in a poorer part of Brazil. They are expected to invest heavily to meet pent-up demand for cellphones, which Telebras has been unable to meet.

Renato Guerreiro, the Communications Ministry's executive sectretary, said the concession winners would pay a total of $5.0-$6.0 billion for licenses and then invest up to $5.0 billion more in new equipment by the end of 1998.
They are also likely to increase the number of cellphone users in Brazil to about six or seven million by the end of next year, up from about two million now, he said.

The B Band program had been in doubt until last week, when Brazil's supreme court ruled, after months of delay and suspense, that the Communications Ministry can act as an interim regulator while a new telecoms law is being approved.
The government also managed to overrule an injunction against the B Band program issued by a court in the state of Bahia which had threatened the concessions plan.
But Monday's opening of the bidding process was not a complete success.

While densely populated areas of Brazil's south and southeast received offers from several groups, there was no bidder for a northern region and only one for the center-west region which covers Brasilia.
By law, concessions cannot be offered to a group without a rival bid being placed.
Executives said the government had discouraged investors from bidding for the northern and center-west regions by setting the minimum license fees too high.
"They're asking a minimum of 660 million reais for Sao Paulo city and 220 million reais for those desolate regions. People think that's too much," said one official who asked not to be named.
